title: Concept-based Adversarial Attack: a Probabilistic Perspective
claim: Perturbing a single input yields little overlap with the target region; modeling a whole concept distribution greatly increases overlap, keeping meaning while still succeeding.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, bottom-to-top flow, colored overlapping density blobs with leader lines to images
description: Two side-by-side panels compare a single-image adversarial attack (left) with a concept-based attack (right). Each shows a pink-red blob for the victim distribution p_vic and a blue blob for the distance distribution p_dis, drawn as nested contour densities. Black lines with dots link blob locations to images. At the bottom are a target-class image (a fish) and the original input. On the left it is a single corgi photo, and on the right it is four corgis in different poses and settings forming the original concept. At the top, adversarial example images have green borders for success and red for failure. On the left the blobs barely touch, so the examples either fail or lose the corgi's meaning. On the right the blobs overlap substantially, and the examples are diverse corgis that all succeed. The eye goes first to the overlapping blobs.
caption: Comparison of a single-image adversarial attack (left) versus our proposed concept-based adversarial attack (right). In both cases, adversarial examples xadv are drawn from the product of a distance distribution pdis and a victim distribution pvic. On the left, pdis is centered on a single image xori, so its overlap with pvic is small. Consequently, adversarial examples that successfully fool the victim classifier typically lose the original image’s meaning, whereas those that preserve the original meaning fail to deceive the classifier. In contrast, on the right, pdis spans the original concept Cori, greatly increasing overlap with pvic. As a result, the generated adversarial examples both maintain the concept’s meaning and easily deceive the classifier. (A green image border indicates an example that successfully fools the classifier; red indicates failure.)
abstract: We propose a concept-based adversarial attack framework that extends beyond single-image perturbations by adopting a probabilistic perspective. Rather than modifying a single image, our method operates on an entire concept - represented by a distribution - to generate diverse adversarial examples. Preserving the concept is essential, as it ensures that the resulting adversarial images remain identifiable as instances of the original underlying category or identity. By sampling from this concept-based adversarial distribution, we generate images that maintain the original concept but vary in pose, viewpoint, or background, thereby misleading the classifier. Mathematically, this framework remains consistent with traditional adversarial attacks in a principled manner. Our theoretical and empirical results demonstrate that concept-based adversarial attacks yield more diverse adversarial examples and effectively preserve the underlying concept, while achieving higher attack efficiency.
